chapter_theme: Hospitality is the reason for having a home and wealth at all. Hosting does not impoverish, refusing it makes a rich person poor, and it depends finally on the face with which a guest is met.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: its excellence (81-82), its fruit in this life (83-85), its fruit in the next (86), the reason for both (87), the fault of neglecting it (88-89), and the need for a pleasant face (90).

81.reading: All of staying at home and living by guarding one's goods is for the purpose of caring for guests and doing them good.
81.nuance: The verse gives household life a purpose outside itself. Parimelazhagar draws the consequence: without this, the toil of home and earning has no fruit.

82.reading: Even if it were the medicine of immortality, eating it alone while the guest stays outside is not to be desired.
82.nuance: Parimelazhagar offers a second, sharper reading as acceptable: if someone calls even one meal eaten without a guest a medicine of immortality, reject it. Either way, the argument sets a refusal to eat alone over the prospect of not dying.

83.reading: The life of one who daily tends the guest who comes will not suffer and fall into ruin.
83.nuance: It answers the obvious worry that hosting every day would be ruinous. Parimelazhagar goes further than the verse's 'not ruined': he says wealth will keep branching out.

84.reading: The fair goddess dwells with a glad heart in the home of one who tends good guests with a glad face.
84.nuance: A chiasm links the two gladnesses: the host's face and the goddess's heart. Parimelazhagar's reason is that she's pleased when her wealth goes the right way. He also takes நல், 'good', to limit the guests to those of high knowledge and conduct.

85.reading: Must one even sow the field of the person who feeds guests and then eats what's left?
85.nuance: மிச்சில், leftovers, is a low word for the host's own food, as if the guest's plate comes first. The rhetorical question doesn't say what the answer is, and the commentators answer it in opposite ways.

positions.position: No sowing is needed, since the field will yield by itself.
Such a host would use even the seed set aside for the field to feed guests.
positions.quote: தன் நிலத்திற்குரிய விதையைக்கூட விருந்தோம்பலுக்குப் பயன்படுத்தாமல் இருப்பானா?

86.reading: One who tends the guest who is leaving and watches for the guest to come will be a good guest to those in the sky.
86.nuance: The host becomes the guest in heaven, and the verse has an elegant reciprocity. Manakkudavar gives 'watching' a concrete rule: not eating without a guest. Kalaignar's 'those in the sky of renown' removes the literal heaven that Parimelazhagar assumes.

87.reading: The fruit of this sacrifice has no set measure: it is as great as the guest's worth.
87.nuance: Calling hospitality வேள்வி claims the language of ritual for a household meal. The measure is the guest and not the cost, and Parimelazhagar supports this with a Naladiyar verse. This also introduces a hierarchy among guests, which sits awkwardly with welcoming whoever comes.

88.reading: Those who don't take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods anxiously and then say 'we have no support'.
88.nuance: It is a late regret: the wealth they guarded with such pain is gone. பற்றற்றேம் can also be read as the renouncer's boast, 'we're without attachment', and that echo seems to me to sharpen the irony, though no commentator here says so.

89.reading: Poverty in the midst of having is the folly that neglects hospitality, and it is found only among fools.
89.nuance: The verse redefines poverty as a failure of use, not a lack of goods. Parimelazhagar explains: since folly takes away the benefit one gets from wealth, it makes having into not having.

90.reading: The anicham flower wilts when smelled, and a guest wilts when the host's face changes on seeing them.
90.nuance: Parimelazhagar's analysis has the guest more delicate than the flower, as the flower needs to be touched but the guest wilts at a distance. He gives a sequence of pleasant face, pleasant word and good deed, which leads directly into the next chapter.

links.note: Amrita is beaten twice in these household chapters: a child's stirred gruel is sweeter than it, and even it isn't worth having while a guest waits. In both, food's worth is decided by who else is at the meal.
Both end in the same phrase, வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு: 81 says the home exists for this, and 212 says wealth earned by effort does. Two different goods are given one purpose.

Here refusal of guests is poverty amid plenty. In 1005, someone with crores is destitute if he neither gives nor enjoys. The later verse widens the charge by also treating failure to enjoy one's wealth as a failure.
The anicham measures the guest here and the beloved in 1111, and both are more delicate than it. The book's most tender image for a lover was first used for a stranger at the door.
